```{r}
#| label: setup

set.seed(4321)

# Options ----------------------------------------------------------------------
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.align = "center")

# Packages ---------------------------------------------------------------------
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tinytable)

# Functions --------------------------------------------------------------------
calculate_or <- function(data) {
  a <- data$Successes[data$Treatment == "A"]
  b <- data$Patients[data$Treatment == "A"] - a
  c <- data$Successes[data$Treatment == "B"]
  d <- data$Patients[data$Treatment == "B"] - c

  (a / b) / (c / d)
}

# Data -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Simpson's paradox example
hospital_data <- tibble(
  Hospital = c("X", "X", "Y", "Y"),
  Treatment = c("A", "B", "A", "B"),
  Patients = c(90, 10, 10, 90),
  Successes = c(80, 9, 1, 30)
)

# UC Berkly admissions data
admissions <- readRDS(here::here("data/ucbadmit.rds"))

# Animal data
animal_data <- readRDS(here::here("data/animal_data.RDS")) |>
  mutate(animal = factor(animal, levels = c("chicken", "rabbit", "cat", "dog")))
```

## Today's question {style="font-size:80%;"}

Can a treatment appear more successful overall, even when it performs worse in
every hospital?


::::: {.fragment .fade-up}
:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}

By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:

- Describe relationships involving three categorical variables.
- Distinguish overall from conditional proportions.
- Explain Simpson's paradox.
- Calculate and interpret odds ratios.
- Explain why accounting for a third variable can change a comparison.

:::

::: {.column width="45%"}

![](assets/homer-simpson.png){.absolute width=251.2px height=348.1px left=668.6px top=38.8px}

:::

::::

## Recap: two categorical variables {style="font-size: 90%;"}

So far, we have considered the relationship between **two categorical variables**.

- Construct contingency tables
- Compare conditional distributions
- Test independence using the chi-squared test
- Examine residuals and measure association strength

:::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: {.callout-important}
## What happens when we introduce a third categorical variable?
:::
::::

## Let's introduce a third variable {style="font-size:95%;"}

[Suppose we want to compare two medical treatments]{.center}

We start with the initial question

::: {.callout-note}
## Is Treatment A more successful than Treatment B?
:::

<br>

:::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Now suppose we also know [which hospital]{.alert} treated each patient.

Our question becomes:

::: {.callout-note}
## Does the treatment comparison look the same within each hospital?
:::
::::

<br>

:::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
The relationship between two variables can look different when we examine it
[within levels of a third variable]{.alert}.
:::
::::

---

## Let's run our example {style="font-size:90%;"}

### The research question

We observe patients receiving [Treatment A]{.alert} or [Treatment B]{.alert}
in two hospitals.

Each patient either experiences [treatment success]{.alert} or
[treatment failure]{.alert}.

We record:

- Hospital
- Treatment
- Number of patients
- Number of successes

We will compare success rates first overall and then within each hospital.

## Let's run our example

### The data

<br>

```{r}
#| label: hospital-data

hospital_data |>
  mutate(
    Failures = Patients - Successes,
    Success_Rate = Successes / Patients
  ) |>
  select(
    Hospital,
    Treatment,
    Patients,
    Successes,
    Failures,
    `Success rate` = Success_Rate
  ) |>
  tt(digits = 3) |>
  style_tt(i = 0, bold = TRUE)
```

A success rate is the proportion of patients who experienced success:

$$
\text{Success rate} = \frac{\text{Number of successes}}{\text{Number of patients}}
$$

---

## First we will ignore the hospital

What happens if we combine all patients receiving each treatment?

<br>

```{r}
#| label: ignoring-hospital
# Group by tratment and ignore hospital
overall_rates <- hospital_data |>
  group_by(Treatment) |>
  summarise(
    Patients = sum(Patients),
    Successes = sum(Successes),
    `Success rate` = Successes / Patients,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Let's look at the success rate
overall_rates |>
  mutate(`Success rate` = scales::percent(`Success rate`, accuracy = 0.1)) |>
  tt() |>
  style_tt(i = 0, bold = TRUE)
```

<br>

:::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: {.callout-note}
## Treatment A has an overall success rate of 81%, compared with 39% for Treatment B.
:::
::::

## But what about the hospital

<br>

```{r}
#| label: patient-dsitribution-1a
hospital_data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Treatment, y = Patients, fill = Hospital)) +
  geom_col(position = "stack", colour = "black", width = 0.65) +
  ggokabeito::scale_fill_okabe_ito() +
  labs(
    x = "Treatment",
    y = "Number of patients",
    fill = "Hospital"
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

<br>

:::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: {.callout-tip}
## Treatment A is used mainly in Hospital X. Treatment B is used mainly in Hospital Y
:::
::::

## Let's consider this in our research question

<br>

```{r}
#| label: hospital-specific-rates
hospital_rates <- hospital_data |>
  mutate(Success_Rate = Successes / Patients) |>
  select(
    Hospital,
    Treatment,
    Patients,
    Successes,
    `Success rate` = Success_Rate
  )

hospital_rates |>
  mutate(
    `Success rate` = scales::percent(
      `Success rate`,
      accuracy = 0.1
    )
  ) |>
  tt() |>
  style_tt(i = 0, bold = TRUE)
```

## Let's consider this in our research question

```{r}
#| label: success-rate
hospital_rates |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = Treatment,
    y = `Success rate`,
    colour = Treatment
  )) +
  geom_point(size = 5) +
  ggokabeito::scale_colour_okabe_ito() +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_percent(),
    limits = c(0, 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Treatment",
    y = "Success rate",
    colour = "Treatment"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~Hospital,
    labeller = labeller(
      Hospital = function(x) paste("Hospital", x)
    )
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

:::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: {.callout-important}
## Treatment B has a higher success rate in **both hospitals**.
:::
::::

## A surprising result {style="font-size:75%;"}

We have found two different conclusions:

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}

### Overall

- Treatment A: 81%
- Treatment B: 39%

[**Treatment A appears better**]{.center}

:::

::: {.column}

### Within each hospital

- Hospital X: B has the higher rate
- Hospital Y: B has the higher rate

[**Treatment B performs better in both**]{.center}

:::
::::

::::: {.fragment .fade-up}
:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}

<br>
<br>

[**Simspons Paradox**]{.center}

:::

::: {.column}

![](assets/homer-simpson.png){fig-align="center"}

:::
::::
:::::

## Simpsons paradox

**Simpson's paradox** occurs when an association between two variables reverses
direction, or otherwise changes substantially, after considering a third
variable.

In our example:

- Treatment A has the higher overall success rate.
- Treatment B has the higher success rate in Hospital X.
- Treatment B also has the higher success rate in Hospital Y.

[The third variable is hospital]{.center}

## Why does this reversal happen

The two treatments are used in different proportions across the hospitals.

- Hospital X has high success rates for both treatments.
- Hospital Y has lower success rates overall.
- Most patients receiving Treatment A are treated in Hospital X.
- Most patients receiving Treatment B are treated in Hospital Y.

The overall success rate therefore reflects both:

1. The treatment-specific success rates.
2. The distribution of patients across hospitals.

## The role of the third variable

<br>

```{r}
#| label: patient-distribution-1b
hospital_data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Treatment, y = Patients / 100, fill = Hospital)) +
  geom_col(position = "stack", colour = "black", width = 0.65) +
  ggokabeito::scale_fill_okabe_ito() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  labs(
    x = "Treatment",
    y = "Number of patients",
    fill = "Hospital"
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

:::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: {.callout-tip}
## The patients receiving the two treatments are not distributed equally across hospitals
:::
::::

---

<br>

```{r}
#| label: animal-plot-1a
animal_data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = size, y = life_expectancy)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 1.5, size = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    x = "Average adult male body mass (kg)",
    y = "Average life expectancy (years)"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

---

<br>

```{r}
#| label: animal-plot-1b
animal_data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = size, y = life_expectancy, colour = animal)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 1.5, size = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  ggokabeito::scale_colour_okabe_ito() +
  labs(
    x = "Average adult male body mass (kg)",
    y = "Average life expectancy (years)",
    colour = "Animal"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```


## Lurking variable {style="font-size:90%;"}

A **lurking variable** is a variable omitted from an initial comparison that
can help explain the observed relationship.

For example:

- Treatment and success are the variables of interest.
- Hospital is a third variable that changes the comparison.

Other examples might include:

- Age when comparing disease rates.
- Department when comparing university admission rates.
- Baseline severity when comparing medical treatments.

:::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: {.callout-important}
## A third variable can exaggerate, weaken, hide or reverse an observed association.
:::
::::

## Now let's talk about odds {style="font-size:95%;"}

Sometimes we want to compare outcomes using odds rather than proportions.

If the probability of success is $p$, the odds of success are

$$
\text{Odds} = \frac{p}{1 - p}
$$

For example, if the probability of success is 0.75:

$$
\text{Odds} = \frac{0.75}{1 - 0.75} = 3
$$

[Or more simply the odds are 3:1]{.center}

## Probability versus odds

<br>

```{r}
#| label: odds-table-1a
tribble(
  ~Probability , ~Odds                  ,
  0.20         , "0.20 / 0.80 = 0.25:1" ,
  0.50         , "0.50 / 0.50 = 1:1"    ,
  0.75         , "0.75 / 0.25 = 3:1"    ,
  0.90         , "0.90 / 0.10 = 9:1"
) |>
  tt() |>
  style_tt(i = 0, align = "c", bold = TRUE)
```

<br>

:::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: {.callout-tip}
## When an event is common, its odds can be substantially larger than its probability.
:::
::::

## Odds ratio {style="font-size:85%;"}

An **odds ratio (OR)** compares the odds between two groups

$$
\text{OR} = \frac{\text{Odds in Group 1}}{\text{Odds in Group 2}}
$$


::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}

## Interpretation

- OR = 1 = Equal odds
- OR > 1 = Higher odds in Group 1
- OR < 1 = Lower odds in Group 1

:::

An odds ratio of 2 means that the odds in Group 1 are [twice]{.alert} those in Group 2.

It does **not** necessarily mean that the probability is twice as high.

## Calculating an odds ratio from a table

Suppose we compare two treatments

```{r}
#| label: odds-table-1b
tribble(
  ~""           , ~Success , ~Failure ,
  "Treatment A" , "(A)"    , "(B)"    ,
  "Treatment B" , "(C)"    , "(D)"
) |>
  tt() |>
  style_tt(i = 0, bold = TRUE) |>
  style_tt(j = 2:3, align = "c")
```

The odds ratio is

$$
OR = \frac{a/b}{c/d} = \frac{ad}{bc}
$$

We call this a [cross-product ratio]{.alert}

## Let's calculate an odds ratio {style="font-size:90%;"}

```{r}
#| label: odds-table-1c
tribble(
  ~""           , ~Success , ~Failure ,
  "Treatment A" ,       80 ,       10 ,
  "Treatment B" ,       60 ,       40
) |>
  tt() |>
  style_tt(i = 0, bold = TRUE) |>
  style_tt(j = 2:3, align = "c")
```


:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}

$$
\text{Odds}_A = \frac{80}{10}=8
$$

:::

::: {.column}

$$
\text{Odds}_B = \frac{60}{40}=1.5
$$

:::
::::


:::: {.fragment .fade-up}


$$
OR = \frac{8}{1.5} \approx 5.33
$$


::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
## The odds of success are approximately 5.33 times as high for Treatment A as for Treatment B in this example.
:::
::::

## How are these useful

We can calculate:

- An overall odds ratio, ignoring hospital.
- An odds ratio within Hospital X.
- An odds ratio within Hospital Y.

These are different summaries of the association between treatment and success.

The key question becomes:

::: {.callout-note}
## Do the treatment odds ratios tell the same story before and after stratification?
:::

## Overall and hospital-specific odds ratios

<br>

```{r}
# Overall odds ratio
overall_or <- hospital_data |>
  reframe(
    Treatment = c("A", "B"),
    Patients = c(
      sum(Patients[Treatment == "A"]),
      sum(Patients[Treatment == "B"])
    ),
    Successes = c(
      sum(Successes[Treatment == "A"]),
      sum(Successes[Treatment == "B"])
    )
  ) |>
  calculate_or()

# Hospital odds ratio
hospital_ors <- hospital_data |>
  group_by(Hospital) |>
  group_modify(~ tibble(OR = calculate_or(.x))) |>
  ungroup()

# Comparison table
tibble(
  Comparison = c("Overall", hospital_ors$Hospital),
  `Odds Ratio` = c(overall_or, hospital_ors$OR)
) |>
  tt(digits = 3) |>
  style_tt(i = 0, bold = TRUE)
```

<br>

:::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
The odds ratios also reverse direction: the overall comparison favours A,
whereas both hospital-specific comparisons favour B.
:::
::::

## Marginal versus conditional associations {style="font-size: 80%;"}

We can describe the two approaches using statistical terminology.

**Marginal association**

- The relationship between treatment and success when hospital is ignored.

**Conditional association**

- The relationship between treatment and success when we compare patients within
  the same hospital.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

### Marginal

All patients are combined.

$$
P(\text{Success}\mid \text{Treatment})
$$

:::

::: {.column}

### Conditional

Patients are compared within hospital.

$$
P(\text{Success}\mid \text{Treatment, Hospital})
$$

:::

::::

## Final takeaway

- A relationship between two categorical variables can change when we
  account for a third variable.
- Simpson's paradox describes a reversal in an association between marginal
  and conditional comparisons.
- Odds ratios provide another way to quantify associations in $2 \times 2$ tables.
- Stratification helps us understand whether an observed relationship
  persists within groups.

::: {.callout-important}
## Next time you compare two groups, ask: could a third variable change the conclusion?
:::

## Introducing the UC Berkeley admissions data

We now move to a real example.

The UC Berkeley admissions data record university applications by:

- Admission outcome
- Gender
- Department

Our initial question is:

**Were male and female applicants admitted at different rates?**

We will then consider whether the department applied to changes our interpretation.
